newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Rifkind to raise POW issue with Japan.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Rifkind to raise POW issue with Japan.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind will discuss with Japan this weekend the plight of Britons who were inmates of Japanese prisoner of war camps during World War Two, a member of parliament said on Thursday.
Opposition Labour MP Denis MacShane said he had been told this at a meeting he and an MP from the ruling Conservatives held earlier in the day with junior Foreign Office minister Jeremy Hanley.

MacShane and Conservative Patrick Nicholls met Hanley to press the government to urge Tokyo to find ways of giving more compensation to former prisoners of war and others maltreated by Japanese soldiers in the camps.
"I am pleased they (the British government) are now taking this seriously," he said.

Rifkind, in Singapore for a meeting between representatives of European Union and South-East Asian nations, will raise the issue at a meeting with Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, MacShane said.

A Foreign Office spokesman said Hanley had told MacShane and Nicholls that the San Francisco Peace Treaty signed in 1951 precluded formal negotiations between the British and Japanese governments on further compensation.

"The Minister said, however, that the government would continue to help in any way it could, including by continuing to impress upon the Japanese government the intensity of feeling in the United Kingdom," the spokesman added.
MacShane said Hanley had agreed to seek "wider legal information" on whether further compensation might be sought for people taken into the camps as children.
Former prisoners of war and civilian internees of the Japanese during World War Two plan to stage a demonstration outside the Japanese embassy in London on Friday.

They said the demonstration, held on the anniversary of the fall of Singapore in 1942, was to show the Japanese the frustration of former prisoners at Tokyo's failure to properly recognise their claims for a full formal apology and for compensation.
"We are fed up with the continuing delays in resolving this matter by the Japanese," said Ann Levick, chairwoman of the Association of British Civilian Internees.
"We want to show them that there is no question of us ever giving up. They have put a shadow over our lives that will not be lifted until justice has been done."
